title: Quantum Chaos and Spread of States in Krylov Subspace: A Topical Review
abstract: Krylov state complexity, or spread complexity, has emerged as a sharp and versatile diagnostic of quantum chaos, information spreading, and many-body dynamics. Built from the Lanczos algorithm and grounded in the optimal-basis theorem, Krylov complexity thereby provides a robust spectroscopic window into quantum dynamics. A central theme is the characteristic overshoot observed in chaotic systems: a complexity peak in which chaotic evolution drives the state deeper into the Krylov chain than in integrable systems before relaxing to equilibrium. This behavior, tied to random-matrix universality classes of spectral statistics, is illustrated across a broad range of models, including quantum billiards, quantum spin chains, and variants of the SYK model. We also discuss proposed holographic descriptions of Krylov complexity in Einstein gravity, and conclude by outlining future directions and open problems, including time-dependent systems and quantum-field-theoretic formulations. A Mathematica notebook is provided for numerical exploration of Krylov complexity and spectral statistics across models.
summary: This review introduces Krylov state complexity as a powerful, general diagnostic for quantifying quantum chaos and information spreading. By utilizing the Lanczos algorithm to map dynamics onto a Krylov subspace, it provides a measure that bridges spectral analysis and real-time evolution. The paper demonstrates its utility across diverse models, from quantum billiards to holographic gravity, highlighting the characteristic 'overshoot' as a key signature of chaotic behavior.
main_problem: The paper seeks a universal diagnostic tool to characterize quantum chaos and the spreading of quantum information across diverse physical systems.
main_result: Krylov state complexity is proposed as a versatile diagnostic that bridges spectral properties and real-time dynamics, revealing characteristic overshoots in chaotic systems.
method: The core method involves constructing the Krylov subspace using the Lanczos algorithm to map the system's dynamics onto a one-dimensional chain, allowing the calculation of state complexity.
model_or_system: The analysis applies to a broad range of quantum systems, including quantum billiards, quantum spin chains, the SYK model, and holographic gravity models (AdS/CFT).
key_observables: Krylov State Complexity (Spread Complexity), Characteristic Overshoot, Spectral Statistics (GOE/GUE), and Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs).
important_parameters: The analysis considers regimes ranging from integrable to chaotic dynamics, and includes both Hermitian and non-Hermitian settings.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that Krylov complexity provides a robust, general diagnostic that complements existing, but incomplete, chaos measures like OTOCs and spectral statistics.
paper_structure: The review progresses by first establishing the need for a general diagnostic, then detailing the formal construction of Krylov complexity via the Lanczos algorithm, and finally applying this tool to various model classes (Hermitian, non-Hermitian, holographic).
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a unified, mathematically rigorous tool (Krylov complexity) to probe chaos and information spreading, connecting spectral theory to real-time dynamics, which is crucial for understanding open quantum systems and many-body dynamics.

Any initial state |ψ0⟩is mapped or projected to the first site (n = 0) of the Krylov chain, KDK |ψ0⟩= (1, 0, · · · , 0)T , and the evolution corresponds to the particle hopping to subsequent sites.

Figure 2 Nearest-neighbor level spacing distributions. The probability density p(s) is shown for the three standard random matrix ensembles (GSE, GUE, and GOE) (red, green, blue) and the integrable Poisson system (black). Histograms represent numerical data obtained by diagonalizing random matrices of dimension 200, with statistics averaged over 50 independent realizations. Solid colored lines denote the corresponding analytical predictions: the exact the Wigner surmise for the Gaussian ensembles (16) and Poisson distribution (17).

Figure 3 Spectral form factor for the random matrix ensembles (GSE, GUE, and GOE) (red, green, blue) and the integrable Poisson system (black). The SFF is evaluated at infinite temperature (β = 0) and plotted on a log-log scale. The numerical curve is generated from matrices of size 200, averaged over 50 realizations. The evolution displays the defining dynamical signatures of quantum chaos for the random matrix ensembles, i.e., the ramp structure: an initial early decay governed by the average density of states, an interruption at the dip time, a subsequent linear ramp reflecting two-level correlations, and a final saturation into a constant plateau.
